en: A Brief Preface to the Commentary on the *Śraddhotpāda-śāstra*:
The One Mind seals all phenomena, and all phenomena are subsumed within the One Mind;

thus, the one and the many are without obstruction, and the sentient being and the Buddha are non-dual—yet this remains beyond the description of brush and ink. Indeed, that which points to the moon may be a finger, but that which crosses the sea cannot be the raft.
Since there is no raft [to cross over], all the sages and worthies have known that the essence of the teachings in this Sahā world consists of the wheel of sound;
through the Samādhi of Illusion, they discourse upon the Mahāyāna, whereby the Sūtras and Śāstras arise in endless succession.

These accumulate to form the Great Canon, which does not exceed the exposition of the One Mind. The Great Being Aśvaghoṣa of Central India, responding to the prophetic decree of the Bhagavat, overturned...
This treatise, which traces the origin of Pāpīyān’s crimson banner back to the true nature (*dharmatā*), is what is called "opening two gates within a single mind.

That the essentials of all scriptures are unified by this one principle—is this not indeed fitting? Translated into one fascicle during the Chengsheng era of the Liang dynasty by the Tripiṭaka Master Paramārtha;
this current translation is that very work. Although the text of the treatise is profound and subtle, even masters of great virtue and high standing...
Because it is difficult to provide a definitive commentary on this work, there are likely not few among the houses of traditional exegesis;

yet nowadays, as for those who transmit it, the *Śūtra-ṭīkā* lacks a core essence, and the record of Master Xuánzàng (Chángshuǐ) lacks breadth—nevertheless, having been passed down for nearly a millennium, they remain beyond reproach.
Recently, the Great Master Hǎnmén of the Ming dynasty extracted the essential points from these two traditions, cross-referencing them with later translations to elucidate what was obscure or subtle.
With every word he utters, he awakens those who study with a cool clarity, causing them to reflect upon the teachings with gentleness and repeated care;

how diligent was Master Han’s intention! My other friend, Longchou, whenever he has leisure from meditative stillness, dwells his mind upon the Indian scriptures, and whenever he encounters even a brief commentary by Master Han, he regards it as a rare treasure.
This summer, in the year of Bingwu, my guest arrived from Dongwei to seek refuge.
During my stay at Zhishan, while by the waters of the White Heron, I once saw the Dragon’s pavilion; therein was nothing else of length, save for a single brief outline.
The Dragon said to me: "I have possessed this outline for many years. Its words are not繁多 (prolix), yet its principles are already stable;
it is especially convenient for beginners. He then entrusted it to a woodblock carver to circulate widely throughout the land, requesting that you compose a preface for it.

Preface: Alas! In these degenerate final times, human talent has become increasingly deficient while books have multiplied; though every household recites them and every family expounds upon them, no one attains true mastery.
Scholars who carry their satchels on their backs suffer from this dilemma. Now, the treatise *Qixin lun* (Awakening of Faith) has been brought forth;

the two masters Xianshou and Changshui have exhausted its source and traced its course to its very end, leaving no further mysteries. By means of this concise commentary, I shall provide a mirror for all.
The two families [of the canon] preserve only one part in a thousand; I fear people may think there are omissions. Longshi said, "Alas, no!
If what you say were true, Master Han’s commentary would be of no benefit to students. To delete the redundant and follow the concise—this is precisely why this commentary was composed.
Those of today have shallow strength and meager talent, lacking the means to penetrate the whole; it is not the fault of the book."

Ji’s error was profound; those who are like "wall-faced" ignoramuses gallop in competition with the "creatures of the earth," recklessly clinging to their own natures and discarding the written word as a model.
They mimic the frowning gestures of Shaolin’s rejection of writing while inviting the laughter of the Great Dharma’s unimpeded freedom.

Indeed, even if the new commentaries of Qinglong were burned and the old bundles of the White Horse [Buddha] were lost, how could the Dharma be transmitted? Consider this deeply; I stand here to establish it.

The abandoned fascicles were exclusively those that had been lost; they were subsequently retrieved from the Shūrin library and transcribed onto long-lived woodblocks. After three months, the work was completed.
Furthermore, I was requested to provide a preface, considering that these words of Master Ryō are indeed indispensable, even if spoken for a particular occasion.
Indeed, when reading this commentary, one must not consider it insufficiently detailed; it serves as a record to precede the first word of the *Jiepan* (Complete Commentary).
On a day in the middle autumn month of the Bingwu year of the Kwanbun era, the śramaṇa Tōmi, having reflected deeply and purified himself,
wrote this with palms joined in the *Kongtei* chamber on Mount Hannyā.
This concludes the first volume of the *Brief Commentary on the Mahāyāna-śraddhotpāda-śāstra*.
The title of this treatise constitutes its fundamental outline. Regarding the phrase "Arisen Faith in the Mahāyāna":
it is spoken because one desires to give rise to correct faith in the Mahāyāna. As for "Mahāyāna," it refers to the essence of the Dharma that is the object of faith.
That which is called "Dharma" is the mind of sentient beings; this mind encompasses all mundane and supramundane phenomena.
Because it possesses the three great meanings of essence (*tǐ*), characteristic (*xiàng*), and function (*yòng*), the "Vehicle" (*yāna*) has the sense of "conveying.
This means that all Buddhas ride upon this to realize *bodhi* and enter *parinirvāṇa*; Bodhisattvas ride upon this to advance toward the ocean of fruition;
and sentient beings ride upon it as they revolve through birth and death. For this mind is the cause and effect of the delusion and enlightenment of all holy ones and ordinary beings.

Because it is the comprehensive characteristic (*sāmānya-lakṣaṇa*) [of all phenomena], the subsequent text states: "It is the essence of the Dharma-gate of the Great Comprehensive Characteristic of the Single Dharma-realm.

Now, because one wishes to faithfully believe that this mind is precisely the correct understanding of the Mahāyāna and is not erroneous, it is called the *Mahāyāna-śraddhotpāda* (Awakening of Faith in the Mahāyāna).
This was because, six hundred years after the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, those with the mindset of the Hīnayāna grasped at phenomena as existing externally and did not believe in "mind-only."
Because non-Buddhist outsiders (tīrthika) give rise to contentious disputes and hold false views that destroy the True Dharma, the Master, moved by compassion, specifically composed this treatise.
Thus, the subsequent causal conditions state: "In order to eliminate doubt and abandon false attachments.

Since doubt and faith are antithetical, if one now believes in this mind, doubt will naturally be eliminated. The commentator (śāstrakāra) discriminates between right and wrong to illuminate the true principle.

Since this work is not a Sūtra or a Vinaya, it is titled a Śāstra. Xianshou’s original commentary was precise and detailed, but because its topical divisions were somewhat disjointed, I have deleted the redundancies and followed a more concise approach.

I have occasionally integrated the meanings of the commentaries without reproducing their texts separately, as my aim was to ensure a coherent, unified whole; thus, it is called the "Abridged Commentary" (Shulüe).
Aśvaghoṣa Bodhisattva composed this treatise.
Regarding the name "Aśvaghoṣa": when this Bodhisattva was first born, a herd of horses neighed piteously, and thus he was named after that.
Furthermore, when he preached the Dharma, all the horses would likewise neigh piteously upon hearing him; hence the commentary [uses] this as its basis.
The *Mahāmāyā-sūtra* states: "Six hundred years after the Tathāgata’s parinirvāṇa, various non-Buddhists (tīrthikas) will arise in competition with their false views to destroy the Buddha-dharma.
At that time, there will be a bhikṣu named Aśvaghoṣa who, skillfully expounding the essential points of the Dharma, will subdue all the non-Buddhists."
The Tripitaka Master Paramārtha translated this;

this is the name of the translator. There are two translations of this treatise: one by the Śramaṇa Paramārtha (translated as "True Meaning") from the country of Ujjayinī in Western India, produced at Hengzhou in the third year of the Chengsheng era of Emperor Yuan of the Liang dynasty.

Translated into one fascicle of twenty-four sheets by Xing Si; translated into two fascicles, also totaling twenty-four sheets, by the Khotanese śramaṇa Śikṣānanda (translated as "Delightful in Learning") during the reign of Empress Wu Zetian of the Great Zhou dynasty at the Foshouji Monastery in the Eastern Capital.
The former translation is currently in circulation.

The *Commentary* was composed by the Śramaṇa Fazang of Taiyuan Monastery in the Western Capital. The *Abridged Version* was compiled by the Śramaṇa Deqing of the Southern Peak (Nanyue). Before composing the main treatise, [the author] first offers a verse of homage and states his intention; subsequently, he presents the main body of the treatise. First, [the homage]: I take refuge in the Buddha, the Great Compassionate One, Who possesses the three bodies and ten powers, And who, out of pity for sentient beings, Manifests in various forms according to their capacities. I take refuge in the Dharma, the wondrous medicine, Which can cure all afflictions; I take refuge in the Sangha, the supreme field of merit, Who practice the path with diligence and vigor. Now, regarding the intent of this work: I have long desired to explain the profound meaning of the *Awakening of Faith*, yet fearing my own shallow wit and limited capacity, I hesitated to undertake it. However, because I am deeply moved by the great compassion of the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas, and wishing to repay the kindness of my teachers and elders, I have ventured to compose this commentary. My hope is that those of future generations who encounter this text may gain entry through these words and thereby realize the ultimate truth. As for the main body of the treatise, it consists of two parts: first, the general exposition of the title; second, the detailed explanation of the text. Regarding the first part: The title of this treatise is *The Awakening of Faith in the Mahāyāna*. "Awakening" refers to the awakening of the mind; "Faith" refers to the faith in the Dharma; "Mahāyāna" refers to the Great Vehicle. These three terms together constitute the title. As for the meaning of the title: "Awakening" signifies the realization of the true nature of the mind; "Faith" signifies the firm conviction in the principle of the One Mind; "Mahāyāna" signifies the vehicle that carries all beings to the other shore. This treatise is intended to clarify the essence of the One Mind and to demonstrate the stages of practice for entering the path. Thus, the title is established to encompass both the goal and the means. [End of section on the title. [The following sections would continue with the detailed explanation of the text.]
I take refuge in all those throughout the ten directions.

Before composing this treatise, it is first necessary to take refuge in the Triple Gem and request their empowerment. The reason for doing so is that this treatise is composed as an exposition of the Sūtras;
the Sūtras were spoken by the Buddha, and the Buddha’s wisdom is profoundly deep, beyond the capacity of ordinary beings to fathom; therefore, I request [the protection of] the Three [Jewels].
Because the power of the Jewel’s majesty protects and sustains him, he is empowered to enter the Buddha-mind through the seal of doctrinal discourse (*dharmārtha-mudrā*).

Furthermore, it is shown that all phenomena have a fundamental source, for the Three Jewels are that which is relied upon as the source. Thus, "taking refuge" (*namas*) refers to the mind capable of returning [to its origin].
To enter the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*), one must first forget the mark of self; since "life" (*jīva*) governs and encompasses the six sense faculties, one now returns with this life.
Thus, the simultaneous extinction of body and mind is the ultimate state of taking refuge. The "ten directions" represent the boundaries of that which is taken as refuge;
this means that the doctrinal principles of the treatise are the very essence of the Dharma-realm (dharmadhātu).
Therefore, one must take refuge in the Triple Gem throughout the ten directions, for since the mind has no limits, its objects are likewise immeasurable.
"O Supreme One, who fully knows all karma, who is unimpeded regarding form, who possesses mastery, the Great Compassionate Savior of the World"—this is the taking of refuge in the Buddha Jewel.

Since the Buddha responds to sentient beings through the three wheels [of body, speech, and mind], the fact that the three wheels here taken as refuge are described as "supreme and most excellent" indicates that this is neither a response-body (*nirmāṇakāya*) nor an enjoyment-body (*saṃbhogakāya*), but rather a reward-body (*vipākakāya*) manifested from the Dharma. "Fully knowing" means...
Mental action (*manas-karman*) is the most supreme. Ordinary beings do not know it; those of external paths have false knowledge of it; Śrāvakas have partial knowledge of it;

Bodhisattvas have knowledge of it in part; only the Buddha knows it universally. Because he realizes the principle through true wisdom (*bhūta-jñāna*), there is no principle that is not thoroughly penetrated;

because he examines the capacities [of beings] through expedient wisdom (*upāya-jñāna*), there is no capacity for which he is not appropriately suited. Therefore, his physical action (*kāya-karman*)—the unimpeded body of mastery—is the most supreme. This is found in the *Avataṃsaka-sūtra* regarding the Buddha.
The marks (*lakṣaṇa*) are immeasurable, and the secondary signs (*anuvyañjana*) are likewise immeasurable; each faculty is perfectly integrated, pervasive, and sovereign.
Furthermore, because the ten bodies (*daśakāya*) are clearly manifest, undestroyed, and unmixed, the Great Compassionate Savior’s vocal activity (*vākkarman*) is supreme.

The Buddha employs the wheel of sound to preach the Dharma in accordance with the capacities of sentient beings; thus, this world of sentient beings is the very place where he is saved by Great Compassion.
Regarding the statement that "among the myriad virtues of the mind capable of saving, the Tathāgata employs only great compassion as his power," this refers to the person [who embodies it].
Furthermore, it points to that body,
its marks, the dharma-nature, the ocean of true thusness, and the treasury of immeasurable merit.
This is the taking refuge in the Dharma Jewel. The word "and" (*ji*) indicates that one not only takes refuge in the Buddha but also in the Dharma.

"That body" refers to the aforementioned Buddha; it means that the Buddha takes the Dharma as his body. This signifies that the teachings flowing from True Suchness (*tathatā*) are themselves the eternally abiding Dharma-body (*dharmakāya*).
Because the complete body of the Tathāgata is already contained within this [Dharma], the intention here is to reveal that this Dharma is itself the Buddha.
Because essence and characteristics are fundamentally non-dual, the "Ocean of the True Suchness of Dharmatā" specifically points to the substance of phenomena (*dharmatā*).
This means that true suchness and dharmatā are the true body of the Dharma-body (*dharmakāya*), universally serving as the essential nature for all defiled and pure phenomena.

Because it remains unchanging while following conditions, and follows conditions while remaining unchanging, it is metaphorically likened to an ocean where wind encounters the water to give rise to various waves.
Because moisture is non-dual and because the Tathāgatagarbha contains and encompasses all virtues, it is called the "Treasury of Merit" (*guṇagarbha*).

"Practicing according to reality," and so forth—this is a refuge in the Sangha Jewel. The Sangha includes both ordinary beings and sages; among sages, there are those of both the Great and Small Vehicles. "Practicing according to reality" refers to the [Bodhisattva] stages (*bhūmi*).
Regarding the phrase "the supreme Bodhisattva," according to the later translation, it reads "the Sangha of Boundless Merit-Treasuries who Diligently Seeks Perfect Enlightenment.
Thus, the first clause praises his virtues; because he is able to encompass all virtues, he is called a "Treasury" (garbha).
The following describes the purpose for composing this treatise:
it is intended to cause sentient beings to eliminate doubt, abandon false attachments, give rise to correct faith in the Mahāyāna, and ensure that the Buddha-seed is not severed.
This constitutes the purpose for composing the treatise. Since phenomena are not established in vain, they must have a specific purpose; herein, there are four such purposes. First:
1. Because those of the two vehicles do not believe in "mind-only," it reveals the true meaning to eliminate their doubts; 2.
Because there are external paths with false attachments, it serves as an antidote to those false attachments to cause them to abandon wrong views; 3.
Because practitioners have not yet initiated correct practice, it analyzes the characteristics of setting out on the path to inspire right faith as the foundation for practice; 4. For...

Because it causes faith to be perfected, enters into and abides in the state of non-retrogression, and renders one capable of receiving the fruit of Buddhahood, it is said that "the lineage of the Buddhas is not severed.
It is for these many reasons that this treatise was composed.
Below follows the actual exposition of the treatise.
The Treatise says: There exists a dharma capable of giving rise to the faculty of faith in the Mahāyāna; therefore, it should be explained.

At the outset, the author of the treatise distinguishes this from the Sūtras and Vinaya, which are not the Dharma spoken directly by the Buddha himself. This refers to the fundamental tenet upon which the treatise relies:
that the single dharma of the one mind possesses two gates and three great meanings. Thus, he correctly demonstrates the Mahāyāna as the primary tenet.
This is called the Mahāyāna because the mental phenomena (citta-dharma) that are its primary object of veneration are themselves the Mahāyāna.
Since there is this supreme benefit in believing that this mind is the root of the Mahāyāna, it must be explained.
The exposition consists of five divisions. What are these five? First, the Division on Causes and Conditions; second, the Division on Establishing the Thesis;
third, the Division on Exegesis; fourth, the Division on Cultivating Faith; and fifth, the Division on Encouraging Practice and its Benefits.

This indicates the rules for its composition; because it divides chapters and analyzes meanings, it is titled "Analysis" (*Vibhaṅga*). Before expounding this treatise, one first establishes five sections as a sequential method:
since phenomena do not arise in isolation, they must have causes and conditions; thus, the first section is on "Causes and Conditions.

Once the causal occasion has arisen, one must indicate the fundamental thesis; thus, the next is "Establishing the Thesis. While the fundamental thesis is the core of the practice, it is not yet an exposition.
Because [the audience] does not understand, it is explained next; since one cannot ascend to the realization of the Dharma’s meaning without practice, the cultivation of faith is presented next;

and although the explanation and practice have been set forth, because those of dull faculties are indolent in their progress, they are exhorted to practice next—this constitutes the primary structural outline of this treatise.
The following is the explanation of the section on causes and conditions (*nidāna*).
First, regarding the inquiry as to what causes and conditions prompted the composition of this treatise, the answer is:
there are eight kinds of such causes and conditions. What are these eight?
To explain the causes and conditions (*hetu-pratyaya*) in brief, there are eight types.

First is the general characteristic of the causes and conditions: namely, it is for the sake of causing sentient beings to leave all suffering behind and attain ultimate bliss, rather than seeking worldly fame, profit, or honor.
Among these eight causes and conditions, the first general characteristic serves as the catalyst for this treatise.

For ordinary beings and non-Buddhists are deluded regarding this single mind, thereby inviting the suffering of birth, the suffering of change, the suffering of conditioned existence, and the suffering of the分段生死 (fen-duan sheng-si, *paricchinna-jāti-maraṇa*).

Furthermore, the Śrāvakas, Pratyekabuddhas, and Bodhisattvas still possess the suffering of 變易生死 (bian-yi sheng-si, *pariṇāmi-jāti-maraṇa*), whereas it is said that the Buddha has realized [the cessation of] it.
The joy of awakening to the Dharma and the tranquility of nirvana are now sought for the purpose of enabling sentient beings to leave suffering and attain happiness,
not for the sake of seeking worldly fame, profit, or honor.
Second, it is because one wishes to explain the fundamental meaning of the Tathāgata so that all sentient beings may understand it correctly without error.

Therefore, this serves as the causal condition for generating [the understanding of] the correct meaning and counteracting false attachments, as presented in the "Section on Establishing the Thesis" and the "Section on Explanation.
This is because those texts state that based on the single dharma of the One Mind, there are two gates, each...
The inclusion of all dharmas is the very root of the Dharma-gates taught by the Tathāgata.

Furthermore, within the gate of arising and ceasing, original enlightenment (*mūla-awakening*) is termed "Suchness" (*tathatā*), while initial awakening (*ādi-awakening*) is termed "Coming. The non-duality of this beginning and this originality is called the "Tathāgata.
Now, because the Tathāgata is established in dependence upon this mind, this mind is designated as the "Root of the Tathāgata"; thus is the meaning fully explained.
This meaning is called "correct understanding" because it corresponds to the contemplative observation (*anvīkṣaṇa*) of the three stages of the noble ones prior to the grounds;
it thus reveals the correct principle. Because this contemplative observation is free from inversion, it is termed "unerring," which serves as the antidote to false attachments.
Third, it is for the purpose of enabling those sentient beings whose roots of goodness have matured to become capable of non-retrogressive faith in the Mahāyāna Dharma.
This constitutes the subsequent analysis of the characteristics of setting out upon the path, as that text states: "It causes those of sharp faculties to set forth."
With resolute faith, one advances toward the Great Way and becomes capable of abiding in non-retrogressive faith;

because this marks the fulfillment of one's own stage at the conclusion of the ten stages of faith, it is called "maturation. One then enters and dwells within the assembly of those established in right determination (*samyaktva-niyāma*), rendering the preceding stages of faith capable of non-retrogression.
Fourth, it is for the sake of causing sentient beings with meager roots of goodness to cultivate faith.
This refers to the four kinds of faith and the four kinds of practice at the beginning of the "Section on Cultivating Faith" (*Xinxing fen*).
As that text states: "To cause those whose faith is not yet fulfilled to cultivate faith so that it becomes fulfilled. Because their faith is not yet...
Because it is already full, it is called "minute"; because it causes one to advance toward fullness, it is called "cultivating faith.

Fifth, it is for the purpose of demonstrating the skillful means to eliminate the obstacles of evil karma, to well protect the mind, to remain far removed from ignorance and pride, and to escape the net of heterodoxy.

Among these, because those with dull faculties are prone to regression and must rely on many skillful means, there are four types. Of these four, the first three constitute the three grades of inferior, middling, and superior;
the last one serves as an exhortation to practice. We shall now begin with the lowest grade, which refers to the fourth section on "Practicing Faith" within the "Lower Level of Practice.
The concluding text of that section states: "It causes those whose karma is heavy and afflictions are numerous to become virtuous..."
For sentient beings whose faculties are difficult to awaken, through skillful means such as ritual prostrations and repentance, their karmic obstructions are eliminated;
because these obstructions have been lightened, they are inwardly freed from stubbornness, stupidity, delusion, and pride, and outwardly they cast off the skeletal nets of malevolent spirits.

Sixth, it is for the purpose of demonstrating the cultivation of *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā* as remedies for the mental faults of ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*) and those of the two vehicles (*dvayayāna*).

This corresponds to the middle grade; specifically, in the fifth section of the "Gate of Cultivating *Śamatha* and *Vipaśyanā*" below, both *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā* are explained together as they dispel the dualistic attachments of ordinary beings and those of the two vehicles, and thus they are termed "remedies."
Seventh, it is for the purpose of demonstrating the skillful means of single-minded mindfulness so that one may be born before the Buddha and attain a faith that is certainly non-retrogressive;
this corresponds to the "Superior Grade. Specifically, at the end of the section on "Cultivating Faith," in the passage titled "Exhorting Birth in the Pure Land," the text states:

"By raising up these superior skillful means, those sentient beings who have attained partial correspondence through contemplation and understanding are feared to encounter the transition of their future retribution [if they do not act now]."
Because retrogression is caused by conditions, it causes one to attain non-retrogression upon rebirth in the Pure Land.
Eighth, it is for the purpose of demonstrating benefits to encourage practice;
this refers to the "Section on Encouraging Practice and Benefits" below, where the text says: "Citing those harms and benefits, he encourages [them] to practice and abandon [the former]."
This serves as a general summary to complete the preceding practices.
There are such causes and conditions for which this treatise was composed. It is asked: "Since these teachings are already fully contained within the Sūtras, why is it necessary to state them again?
The answer is: "Although these teachings exist within the Sūtras, because the faculties and conduct of sentient beings [differ]..."

Regarding the distinction between those who equally receive and understand [the teaching] based on conditions: it need not be discussed if, while the Tathāgata is in the world, sentient beings possess sharp faculties, there is a speaker of superior physical, mental, and karmic qualities, and a single utterance of the perfect voice is understood differently by various types of beings.

The following section clarifies whether it is necessary or unnecessary to provide an explanation. This statement refers to the period of the True Dharma (*saddharma*), when the Buddha was manifest in the world;
because the Tathāgata personally preached the Dharma for them, there was no need for an explanation. The "perfect sound of form and mind" refers to the excellence of the Buddha’s three karmas.
Regarding this perfect sound, there are two meanings. As the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* states: "The Tathāgata, in..."
Within a single utterance, one expounds an infinite ocean of sūtras; because the Tathāgata’s voice is identical to all sounds, it is called the "Perfect Sound" (*paripūrṇa-svara*).
It is also said that through a single word, one expounds the linguistic dharmas of all sentient beings without exception;
for all sounds are this one sound, and this one sound is all sounds—each and every utterance pervades and exhausts the realms of living beings.

The realms [of sound] are such that their phonemes and rhythms are never confused; if the sound were not pervasive, it would not be perfect, and if the sound were pervasive but lacked rhythmic modulation, it would not be perfect sound.
Now, without destroying the modulation, it is equally pervasive; without moving from its pervasiveness, it possesses distinct rhythms.
This is the Perfect Sound of the Tathāgata, which is not within the realm of mental consciousness or discursive thought.
If, after the parinirvāṇa of the Tathāgata, there are sentient beings who are able to attain understanding through extensive hearing by means of their own power—

understanding the Buddha’s intent upon hearing the extensive scriptural text without requiring other treatises— it is said they possess "their own power. This constitutes both the upholding of the text (*dhāraṇī*) and the upholding of the meaning (*artha*).
There may also be sentient beings who, by their own power, understand much despite hearing little;
because they too can seek out the brief scriptural texts through their own power and deeply comprehend the Buddha’s intent,
there is likewise no need for them to maintain this in meaning or maintain it in the words.
There may be sentient beings who lack the power of their own minds and attain understanding only by means of extensive treatises.

Such individuals rely solely on the scriptural texts and cannot comprehend the underlying meaning; because they attain clear understanding only through the extensive treatises of others, it is said that they "lack the power of their own minds.
These individuals possess the retention of the words (*dhāraṇī*) but not the retention of the meaning.

There are sentient beings who, finding extensive treatises cumbersome due to their voluminous length, prefer concise summaries that condense many meanings into few words and are able to grasp the understanding from them.
This clarifies those for whom the teaching is appropriate (*yathābhavyatā*).
There is no need for extensive treatises for two reasons: first, because their faculties are sharp, they do not require a dualistic mind [to comprehend].
It is troublesome and intolerable.
Thus, this treatise should be expounded in order to comprehensively encompass the boundless meanings of the Tathāgata’s vast and profound Dharma.

This clarifies that the meaning of this treatise is profound and vast. Taking the single dharma of the one mind as the essence of the great general characteristic (mahāsāmānyalakṣaṇa) of the Dharma-realm, it penetrates to the source of the Dharma-realm;

hence it is called "profound. Because it encompasses boundless dharmas, it is called "vast. "Profound" refers to the wisdom of suchness (yathābhūtajñāna), while "vast" refers to the wisdom of phenomena (yāvadbhāvajñāna).
Having already explained the section on causes and conditions, next we shall explain the section on establishing the doctrine. Regarding the Mahāyāna, it is generally said to be of two kinds.
What are these two? First, the phenomena (dharma); second, the meaning (artha).
This is the section on establishing the thesis (*pratijñā*). "Dharma" refers to the essence of the Mahāyāna, which is the fundamental principle (*mūla-dharma*).
Its primary status lies in the causal stage (*hetu*), where it encompasses both the defiled and the pure; in the resultant stage (*phala*), it refers exclusively to the pure.

"Meaning" (*artha*) refers to the analysis of the name and meaning of the Mahāyāna. Why is this mind called "Great" (*mahat*)? It is because this mind possesses the three great meanings; therefore, it is named "Great."
Because there are two modes of operation, it is called a "vehicle" (*yāna*); for this reason, the essence of the Dharma is first revealed, followed by the explanation of its principles.
That which is called "Dharma" refers to the mind of sentient beings; this mind encompasses all mundane and supramundane dharmas.
Based upon this mind, the meaning of the Mahāyāna is manifested.
This indicates the fundamental tenet and clarifies the meaning. To bring forth the essence of this Dharma, it says:

"The mind of sentient beings" refers to the *tathāgatagarbha*-mind, which possesses two gates—the gate of conjunction and the gate of non-conjunction. Because it exists in the state of sentient beings, it accords with defilement and thus possesses both gates.

What are these two? First, emptiness as it truly is, because it can ultimately manifest reality;
second, non-emptiness as it truly is, because it possesses its own essence, which is fully endowed with the qualities of untainted nature.
This explains the two meanings of the inquiry and the response. Regarding "emptiness as it truly is" (*yathābhūta-śūnyatā*):
this refers to the emptiness within reality itself that is devoid of false defilements; it does not mean that reality itself is empty. This is the emptiness of reality.

Because it is empty of the false, it is able to manifest the true principle; therefore, it is called "manifesting reality. There are two meanings to its being "not empty": first, it is distinct from the false and lacks [independent] substantiality.

Therefore, because it is distinct from the two types of outflows (*āsrava*) and the afflictions (*kleśa*) that are as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, it is said to be "fully endowed" and so forth.

A verse in the *Buddhatva-śāstra* states: "Because adventitious dust is empty, it is separated from the dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*); the unsurpassed Dharma is not empty, and thus it accords with the dharma-realm."
That which is called "emptiness as it truly is" (yathābhūta-śūnyatā) refers to its non-conformity with all defiled phenomena (*saṃkleśa-dharma*) from the very beginning;
that is to say, because it is free from the differentiated characteristics of all phenomena and because it is devoid of false mental conceptions.
This is a brief explanation of the meaning of emptiness (*śūnyatā*). Because delusory objects arise from delusory thoughts, it is explained to reveal their non-existence.

This is because the inverted mind and delusory objects exist in terms of mental attachment but lack objective reality; whereas the virtue of *tathatā* (suchness) exists in terms of objective reality but lacks mental attachment.
Therefore, they do not correspond.

One should know that the self-nature of true thusness (tathatā) is neither characterized by existence nor characterized by non-existence; it is neither characterized by what is not existence nor characterized by what is not non-existence;

it is neither characterized by both existence and non-existence, nor by a single characteristic, nor by diverse characteristics, nor by what is not a single characteristic, nor by what is not diverse characteristics, nor by both a single and diverse characteristics.
This is an extensive explanation of the meaning of emptiness. The phrase "not having characteristics" clarifies that the truth is free from false existence.
A deluded person says: "If it is not existent, then it must be non-existent. Therefore, the explanation states: "It is not non-existent.

Upon hearing the preceding "neither existent nor non-existent," the deluded person claims that this double negation is itself the True Suchness (*tathatā*). The explanation states: "I speak because of your attachment to a self."
"It is neither existent" does not mean that the essence of phenomena (*dharmatā*) is non-existent; it is because you maintain "existence" while I maintain "non-existence" that [I say this].
Nor does "neither" mean that the essence of phenomena is not non-existent. Furthermore, this is not a mere negation of both. The deluded one says:

"I previously established existence and established non-existence, whereas you establish 'neither. If this 'neither' persists, then existence and non-existence must perish. Now, since this "neither" is already...
Regarding the statement "it is neither mine nor non-existent," the commentary further explains: "Because you cling to the 'neither-nor' (ubhayābhāva), I say it is 'not not-not.

How can you accept the 'neither-nor' while still clinging to the simultaneous presence of both characteristics? This is because deluded people take the four positions (*catuṣkoṭi*) to be the true nature of reality (*tathatā*);

therefore, the word "not" (*na*) is used specifically to refute them. As it is said, once the four positions are transcended, the hundred negations (*śata-apavāda*) are all dispelled. [This applies to] identity and difference.

The four propositions [of existence, non-existence, both, and neither] may be understood according to the preceding analysis. Although there are many ways of grasping, they are all subsumed within these two sets of four propositions;

thus, the *Śata-śāstra* states: "Furthermore, in order to demonstrate that all phenomena grasped by the world are not real, and to show that the graspings of the non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*) are inconsistent, the verse says: 'Existence, non-existence, both, and neither—none of these are one.'"
The two pairs are matched in sequence, yet the wise realize they are not real.

To speak of them collectively, it is said that because all sentient beings possess a deluded mind that discriminates from moment to moment, these [phenomena] are all non-corresponding and are therefore called "empty.
If one is free from the deluded mind, there is truly nothing that can be empty.

This concludes the meaning of emptiness (*śūnyatā*). Because false conceptualizations regarding the sands of the Ganges are too numerous to enumerate exhaustively, they are now collectively subsumed and analyzed as being non-associated.
This follows the formal conclusion (*nigamana*). For those who have abandoned delusion, this is the reverse of the conclusion. Regarding the defiled, one does not speak of the real as being empty;
rather, it is taken as empty because its essence is such that it is not [substantially] existent. Furthermore, this passage serves to resolve a doubt. As for the doubter, having heard...
If one were to negate true substance and the ocean-like merits by asserting ultimate emptiness, this commentary would be undertaken;
thus, hearing of emptiness would not differ from hearing of non-emptiness.
The explanation of the meaning of emptiness is concluded above. Below follows the explanation of the meaning of non-emptiness.
What is called "not empty" refers to the fact that the essence of phenomena has already been revealed as empty and devoid of falsehood;
it is the true mind, eternally constant and unchanging, in which pure dharmas are fully perfected—this is what is termed "not empty."
This reveals the meaning of "not empty. "Constant, eternal, and unchanging" refers to the vertical manifestation of the true essence, which is infinite throughout the three periods of time;

this explains the previous point that it possesses its own intrinsic nature. "The fulfillment of pure dharmas" refers to the horizontal manifestation of pure virtues, which are inexhaustible throughout the ten directions;

this reveals the previous point that it is fully endowed with untainted [dharmas] and so forth. Since its intrinsic nature is both constant and unchanging, it further possesses these untainted qualities.
If the essence of the dharma of merit were thus, how could it be empty? Therefore, it is concluded that it is not empty.
Furthermore, there are no marks to be grasped, because this realm is free from conceptual thought and can only be realized through personal verification.
This explains away doubts. Those who are deluded, upon hearing that pure dharmas are not empty, claim they are identical to the existence of emotional attachments;
this passage is intended to refute such a view. Thus, "not empty" is not different from "empty," because it is free from the characteristics explained below.

If false thoughts were capable of being objects of perception, then there would be characteristics; since [pure dharmas] are known to be solely the domain of true wisdom, it is clearly understood [that they are devoid of characteristics].
Because there is no characteristic of false attachment, it is said that "only through realization is there correspondence.
The above concludes the explanation of the Section on the Suchness of Mind. Below follows the explanation of the Section on the Arising and Ceasing of Mind, which consists of two major divisions.
First, the explanation of the mind and dharmas subject to arising and ceasing; second, the discernment of the meaning demonstrated therein. Within the first section, there are two parts:
first, the arising and ceasing of the defiled and the pure; second, the mutual relationship between the defiled and the pure. For now, we address the first.
Regarding the arising and ceasing of the mind: because it relies upon the *tathāgatagarbha*, there is a mind that arises and ceases.

The following explains this mind of arising and ceasing; first, it indicates its essence. This means that because the non-arising and non-ceasing mind is moved by the wind of ignorance, it functions as arising and ceasing;
therefore, the mind of arising and ceasing is said to rely upon the non-arising and non-ceasing mind. Thus, these two minds are ultimately [one].
There is no dual substance; it is merely spoken of as being mutually dependent in terms of two meanings.

Just as unmoving water, when blown by the wind, becomes moving water—wherein movement and stillness differ, yet the substance of the water is one—so too is the intrinsically pure mind called the *tathāgatagarbha*.
Because it moves and produces arising and ceasing due to the wind of ignorance, it is said to "depend upon the *tathāgatagarbha*."
There is a mind characterized by arising and ceasing.
That which is called "neither arising nor ceasing" is conjoined with this arising and ceasing, being neither identical to it nor different from it.
This distinguishes the characteristics of arising and ceasing; it is the activity of the Tathāgatagarbha, the intrinsically pure mind, manifesting as arising.

Because cessation and non-separation [of arising and ceasing] constitute harmony, it is called "conjunction" (*sāmagrī*); this does not mean that there are separate arising and ceasing that come to unite with True Suchness (*tathatā*).
Rather, it means that the mind of arising and ceasing and the arising and ceasing of the mind are of one and the same characteristic.

Since the non-arising and non-ceasing of the mind becomes the mind of arising and ceasing due to ignorance, it arises from original enlightenment (*mūlapratyavekṣaṇajñāna*) without having two distinct natures; they do not abandon or separate from one another.

Therefore, the subsequent passage states: "It is like the water of the great ocean, which, due to the wind, moves in waves; the characteristics of the water and the characteristics of the wind do not abandon one another.

This means that the true mind, in its entirety, manifests as the characteristic of birth-and-death; yet these characteristics of birth-and-death are none other than spiritual understanding (*vijñapti*), never departing from the true mind.
Thus, this non-separation is called 'harmony' (*sāmagrī*). That it is neither identical nor different refers to True Suchness (*tathatā*)."
Because the whole moves, the mind and its arising-and-ceasing are not different from it; yet because it is the eternally unchanging true nature, it is not identical with arising-and-ceasing.

According to the *Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra*, the defiled dharmas of the seven consciousnesses constitute arising-and-ceasing, while the pure dharma of the Tathāgatagarbha constitutes non-arising-and-non-ceasing.
These two are combined to form the ālayavijñāna, and they are so called because of this combination.
They are neither identical nor different; for if they were identical, there would be no combination, and if they were different, there would likewise be no combination.
Because they are neither identical nor different, combination is possible. As the Sūtra says: "For example, a lump of clay and its subtle particles are neither different nor not different;
so too it is with golden ornaments. If the lump of clay and the subtle particles were different... [the following portion of the original text is omitted].

That which is produced by them is in fact produced by them; therefore, they are not different. If they were not different, there would be no distinction between a lump of clay and its subtle particles.

Likewise, if the evolving consciousnesses (*pravṛtti-vijñāna*) and the storehouse consciousness (*ālaya-vijñāna*) were different in their true nature, the storehouse consciousness would not be their cause.
If they were not different, then when the evolving consciousnesses cease, the storehouse consciousness should also cease; yet its own true nature does not, in fact, cease.
Therefore, it is not the characteristic of self-nature that ceases, but rather the characteristic of activity that ceases. The commentary explains:
herein, "self-nature" refers to the *tathāgatagarbha*, while "transformative consciousnesses" refer to the seven consciousnesses and the "store-consciousness" (*ālayavijñāna*).

Now, the author of this treatise, summarizing the contextual meaning of the preceding and following passages of that sutra, establishes this position; thus he says they are "neither identical nor different."
It is named *ālayavijñāna*. This is a name for the arising and ceasing of this [consciousness]. The meaning of "this arising and ceasing" and "non-arising and non-ceasing" is not one;
yet the mind that discerns them is not different from them. This mind in which these two meanings are non-dual is named *ālayavijñāna*, or as it is also called, *ālaya*.

*Ālaya* is merely a transliteration of the Sanskrit sound. The Tripiṭaka Master Paramārtha of the Liang dynasty translated it according to the name as "the consciousness that does not perish" (*wumoshishi*).

Now, Dharma Master Xuanzang translates it according to its meaning as "storehouse consciousness" (*zangshi*). "Storehouse" (*zang*) has the sense of "gathering and storing," while "not perishing" (*wumosheng*) has the sense of "not being lost.
Thus, the meaning is identical though the names differ. That which is gathered is called a "storehouse," referring to how all sentient beings grasp it as [their self].

For this reason, because the true mind does not abide in its own nature but, through the harmony of perfuming, appears as if it were unitary and permanent, the deluded take these appearances for reality and grasp them as an internal self.
Since this is subsumed under the view of self (*ātma-dṛṣṭi*), it is called the "store" (*ālaya*).
For this reason, at the stage where the two kinds of self-view never arise again, the name "ālayavijñāna" is lost. Furthermore, it can...
It is called "ālaya" because it stores its own essence within all phenomena and can also store all phenomena within its own essence; as the treatise states:
"it is that which stores, that which is stored, and that which is clung to with self-love"—this is what is meant. It is based on this meaning that the name is established.
This consciousness has two meanings;

this is the explanation of its meaning. As for the two meanings: it is because the substance of this consciousness is fundamentally formed by the union of the true and the delusive that, while currently in a state of delusion, it fully contains these two meanings.
Regarding True Suchness (*tathatā*), there are two meanings: first, the meaning of immutability; second, [the meaning of adaptability].
